# The AI Data Centre Legal Case That Could Eradicate Civil Rights

## A lawsuit that at first was a conflict over clean air is turning into a fight over civil rights. And the Trump administration has teams up with Elon Musk’s SpaceX to challenge a fundamental right of US citizens.

--

Listen

Share

In April 2026, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), the civil rights organisation formed in 1909 that once had Thurgood Marshall fighting against segregation, filed a lawsuit against SpaceX/xAI’s data centres in Memphis, Tennessee over alleged unpermitted use of gas turbines.

What could have been a simple case about air pollution has now , after the involvement of the Trump administration, turned into a fight over the right to sue the industry at all. The outcome of this case could have severe implications not only for environmental law, but also for the enforcement of the Civil Rights Act.

### Background

Since 2025, Elon Musk’s xAI (now part of SpaceX) has been building its AI data centres in Memphis Tennessee. However, as many other data centre projects xAI found it challenging to connect the data centre to the power grid and therefore opted for the solution to essentially build their own power plant in the form of giant gas turbines.

Those gas turbines emit NOx (shorthand for nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide), and a lot of it. SpaceX did however not seek a permit to operate them, claiming that being a “temporary installation”, no permit was required, facts that the NAACP disputes:

> “Move fast and break things” is the unofficial motto of the tech industry. As the motto promises, artificial intelligence company Defendant X.AI Corp. (“xAI”) and its subsidiaries broke Clean Air Act requirements that protect public health when rushing to build gas power plants for their “Colossus” data centers in the greater Memphis area. […] Indeed, xAI and its subsidiaries have tried to outrun the Clean Air Act by repeatedly building gas power plants for these data centers — in communities in the greater Memphis area with significant Black populations — without obtaining mandatory permits. (NAACP complaint)

NAACP lays out that the pollution emitted by the gas turbines is harmful to the population in the area, not limited to the state of Tennessee.

> The Colossus Gas Plant emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants, including nitrogen oxides (“NOx ”) and formaldehyde, which are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers in persons exposed to them. These emissions do not stop at the Mississippi state line; Tennessee residents are also exposed. (NAACP complaint)

The NAACP represents mostly black neighbourhoods, which are located right across the border in Mississippi, and, according to the NAACP filing, are especially affected by the emissions.

> Tens of thousands of people, including members of Plaintiffs NAACP and NAACP Mississippi State Conference (“NAACP MS”), live, worship, study and work in the homes, churches, and schools that immediately surround the Colossus Gas Plant, and hundreds of thousands more live in the greater Memphis area. A much larger share of this population is Black than that of the country’s population as a whole. (NAACP complaint)

### Where is the EPA?

While one could think that if xAI has violates the Clean Air Act, the EPA, after all the agency responsible for enforcing environmental law, would become active. It did not.

So the NAACP, as is its right, took maters in their own hand.

The right to do so stems from the fact that Congress has made special provisions (“citizen-suit provisions”) for civil actors to take action themselves against the industry if the state or agency do not. The reason Congress (wisely) did so should be obvious: The provision exists as a safeguard against any collusion of the government with the industry against the interest of the civil society. In other words, Congress did not trust the administration to enforce the law alone.

When amending the Clean Air Act in 1970, Congress indeed took the inspiration for those citizen-suit provisions from similar legislation in the civil rights arena, the possibility for citizens to bring lawsuit against violators or government agencies to enforce environmental laws. Similar provisions therefore were added elsewhere, such as to the Clean Water Act.

It is this provision that the Trump administration, together with SpaceX, now wants to invalidate and declare unconstitutional.

### The Intervention

On 15 June the Trump administration filed a motion to intervene in the lawsuit. This in itself is not unusual, and it is indeed common and perfectly within the right of the government to do so when environmental legislation is involved. In many cases, one could expect the EPA itself to intervene on behalf of the plaintiffs, or to clear up misunderstanding about the environmental permission process.

Here though, the Trump administration intervened with a bang: For a start, it declared the SpaceX data centre to be of importance for “national security”. Not only did it point out that Grok AI, the infamous Chatbot by xAI also known for its generation of nonconsensual sexual imagery, is being used by the US military, it even went into details:

> For example, during Operation Epic Fury, Grok (through the Department’s Maven Smart Systems) “enabled U.S. forces to deploy over 2,000 munitions to 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours ... , a testament to the greatly increased operational efficiency made possible by the Grok Gov Model.” (MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT re 58 MOTION to Intervene 15 June)

This is quite an astonishing admission: Many have speculated to what extent and with the help of what tools the US military utilised AI in the war against Iran, including in the strike against a girls’ school ⁠in Minab, said ​to have killed 150 students. Now we have a hint: It might have been Grok by SpaceX.

While we can’t be absolutely sure, but could this use of Grok might have been just the kind of “autonomous weapons” and targeting that let to the fallout between the US Department of Defense and Anthropic ?

If the governments claim that the Memphis data centres are crucial to run Grok, considering that xAI has now rented out that compute power to Anthropic (Howley 2026), is a valid question, but likely won’t play a role in the lawsuit.

In any case, the Trump administration claims that both the national interest (security), and the state’s interest, overwrite the NAACP’s claim, by simply stating that if NAACP was successful in court it “would create an immediate and substantial disruption of the State’s economy”.

Never mind that “a State’s economy” is still bound by environmental law, if it likes it or not, claiming that the shutdown of a single data centre in Memphis would “disrupt” the economy of Mississippi, a state where the data centre isn’t even located, seems rather bold.

### Prosecutorial discretion … of the President?

But then the Trump administration goes all in:

Not only should the court dismiss the lawsuit outright for reasons of “federal policy, national security, and the public interest”, it even claims that NAACP should not even have the chance to object to the dismissal, which according to the Trump administration, is solely a question of its own “prosecutorial discretion”.

It is further claiming that all “citizen-suit provisions” are “constitutionally questionable” and collide with the President’s article II powers, which has become a recent favourite of the administration (and the US Supreme Court) to shift power from Congress to the president:

### In plain language

What does all this mean in plain language?

- The Trump administration claims that because xAI’s Grok is essential for national security, hence it overrides environmental regulation.

- NAACP lawsuits should be dismissed outright and with prejudice (meaning NAACP could not bring it again, ever) because the citizen-suit provisions in the Clean Air Act is unconstitutional

- The Trump administration solely has the right to decide what lawsuits can be brought against violators in the industry.

To make it clear what that means: If a company would establish an illegal waste dump next to your house, you would not have the right to file a lawsuit if the US administration sees no reason to act.

### The civil rights implications

As mentioned above, the citizen-suit provisions in the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act are modelled after the Civil Rights Act. If the Trump administration claims that those are unconstitutional, why would they stop at environmental regulation? They will certainly extend this claim to lawsuits brought under the Civil Rights Act.

### Is all of this a deliberate setup?

Now here we can only speculate. At first, xAI builds a data centre in a mainly black neighbourhood, does not bother to ask for environmental permits, likely aware that the EPA will not take action and if a lawsuit is being filed, the government will come to the rescue. Was xAI looking for this fight? Meanwhile, the Trump administration jumps at the chance to not only (again) move powers from Congress to the president, but also rid itself of those pesky citizen lawsuits brought to enforce the law.

Now I assume the chances that a district judge declares the citizen-suit provisions unconstitutional are slim, but for the Trump administration that is not the point. If they lose the case, and likely they expect to do so, it can bring it all the way up to the US Supreme Court. Teaming up in this with Elon Musk seems too good to be true for the administration. Other companies might not want to be associated with such an obvious political motivated attempt to limit civil right.

It is worth noting that this is not the first time this year the Trump administration has intervened on behalf of Elon Musk: Only a few month ago it intervened in xAI’s lawsuit against the State of Colorado over its AI regulation that attempted to ban ”algorithmic discrimination”. While Colorado backtracked before this could be properly decided, both xAI and the administration made a constitutional argument (Collier et al. 2026).

### Conclusion

The importance of this case can hardly be overstated. Not only has the Trump administration made it clear that wherever it sees fit (or is colluding with parts of the industry) it will attempt to squash citizen suits, but also that it considers those lawsuits unconstitutional and a violation of the President’s Article II powers.

That of all companies Elon Musk’s SpaceX is the defendant in this case, with its unlimited financial resources and little regard for public image, seems just too convenient to be a coincidence.

Civil Rights are only worth something if they can be claimed and enforced. The citizen-suit provisions are essential to do so.
